traveler: Francis of Assisi (Francesco di Pietro di Bernardone)
title: The Life of Saint Francis: from the Stall of Assisi to Sister Death
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Assisi, the stall of San Francesco il Piccolino
stops.campa: In the stall beside the merchant's house, while Pietro di Bernardone trades cloth in France, the lady Pica Bourlémont is delivered of a son. In pregnancy she was given a vision that the boy would be a great spiritual leader, and a pilgrim's word that he must be born among the beasts, like the Lord; so she emptied the ground floor into a manger, hay strewn, an ox and an ass led in, and the child is born into a performance of Bethlehem, the first presepe, staged by his mother. She names him Giovanni, after the Baptist. Assisi keeps the little vault to this day.
suggested_refs: Oratory of San Francesco Piccolino, Assisi, the traditional birth-stall with its 14th-century inscription
sources: Arnaldo Fortini, Nova Vita di San Francesco

stops.name: Assisi, Cathedral of San Rufino, the baptism
stops.campa: The infant is carried up the hill to San Rufino, cathedral of the martyr-bishop of Assisi, and baptized Giovanni at the great Romanesque font, his mother's name for him, given for the Baptist. When Pietro rides home from France he will overrule the font and call the boy Francesco: for her French culture, the troubadour poetry, the exquisite cloth of Provence, and the family Bourlémont. A stranger, some say an angel in pilgrim's dress, asks to hold the child, and presses a mark like a cross into his right shoulder before vanishing. The same font will later christen Clare di Favarone.
suggested_refs: The baptismal font of San Rufino, Assisi, still in use
sources: Arnaldo Fortini, Nova Vita di San Francesco

stops.name: Assisi, Piazza del Comune, king of the revels
stops.campa: Francesco, now the richest young man of the piazza, spends his father's florins faster than the shop earns them. He is elected master of the revels, carries the baton of the tripudianti, and leads the youth of Assisi through the streets at night singing the songs of the troubadours in French. He dresses in parti-colored silks, sews sackcloth to fine cloth for a joke, feeds every table. Celano says he was the first in follies, and yet courteous beyond all of them, and already unable to refuse a beggar who asked for the love of God.
suggested_refs: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima I.1-2, the portrait of the vain young merchant

stops.name: Collestrada, the battle with Perugia
stops.campa: War between Assisi and Perugia. Francesco rides out in armor with the commune's cavalry to the hill of Collestrada above the Tiber crossing, and there in November 1202 the men of Assisi are broken and slaughtered; the chroniclers say the fields were red down to Ponte San Giovanni. Because his armor shows him worth a ransom, Francesco is not butchered with the foot-soldiers but taken alive, roped, and marched to Perugia. He is twenty years old and has seen the face of war.
suggested_refs: The hill of Collestrada between Perugia and Ponte San Giovanni, the battlefield

stops.name: Perugia, the year in the pits
stops.campa: A year in the underground prisons of Perugia. His fellow captives, nobles of Assisi, sink into rage and melancholy; Francesco alone laughs and sings in his chains, until they think him mad. He befriends the one knight so bitter that all the others shun him. When they ask how he can rejoice in a Perugian pit, he gives them the first prophecy of his life, and the canon records it. Fever takes hold of him in the damp; by the time his father ransoms him, late in 1203, he is a sick man.
stops.quote: What do you think will become of me? You will see that one day I shall be adored by the whole world.
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 4
suggested_refs: Legend of the Three Companions, the prison prophecy

stops.name: Assisi, the sickbed and the stale world
stops.campa: Long illness after the ransom. When Francesco can walk again he goes out leaning on a stick to look at the countryside he loved, the vines, Subasio, the plain toward Foligno, and finds to his astonishment that none of it gives him any joy. The beauty of the fields has gone flat, and he wonders at the change in himself, Celano says, and begins to despise what he had admired. The sickness of the body has opened a crack in the merchant's son through which another life is already looking in.
suggested_refs: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima I.3, the convalescent walk

stops.name: Spoleto, the dream of the arms
stops.campa: Restored, Francesco buys splendid armor to ride south to Apulia and win knighthood in the wars under Walter of Brienne. He gets no farther than Spoleto. In the night a voice comes to him in a dream that has already shown him a palace hung with arms: 'Who can do more for you, the lord or the servant?' 'The lord,' he answers. 'Then why do you leave the lord for the servant?' Francesco asks the question that unmakes his knighthood, hears 'Go home; it shall be shown you what to do,' and at dawn turns his horse back toward Assisi.
stops.quote: Lord, what do you want me to do?
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 6
suggested_refs: The Dream of the Palace, Giotto cycle, Upper Basilica of San Francesco, Assisi

stops.name: The plain below Assisi, the kiss of the leper
stops.campa: Riding on the plain near the lazar-house of San Lazzaro d'Arce, Francesco meets the thing he loathes most in the world: a leper, standing in the road. Everything in him recoils; nothing in him obeys. He dismounts, puts money in the ruined hand, and kisses it, and the leper gives him the kiss of peace in return. When he has ridden on and looks back, the canon says, the open plain is empty. In his Testament, dying, he dates his whole life from this road.
stops.quote: When I was in sin, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers. And the Lord Himself led me among them, and I showed mercy to them. And when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me was turned into sweetness of soul and body.
stops.quote_source: Testament of St. Francis, 1226
suggested_refs: The Testament of St. Francis; the site of the leprosarium of San Lazzaro d'Arce on the Assisi plain

stops.name: Rome, the beggar's rags at St. Peter's
stops.campa: On pilgrimage to the tomb of the Apostle, Francesco watches the pilgrims drop small coins through the grate and, disgusted at their meanness toward the Prince of the Apostles, flings in his whole purse with a crash that turns every head. Outside in the portico he borrows the rags of a beggar, gives the man his own clothes, and stands all day among the poor of St. Peter's with his hand out, begging in French for the joy of it. He is rehearsing, in borrowed rags, the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Old St. Peter's Basilica, the atrium of the beggars

stops.name: San Damiano, the crucifix speaks
stops.campa: In the half-ruined chapel of San Damiano below the walls, Francesco kneels before a painted Byzantine crucifix. The lips of the image part and the crucified Christ speaks to him by name, three times: 'Francis, go and repair my house, which as you see is falling wholly into ruin.' He takes the command with a merchant's literalness: stones, mortar, this chapel, not yet knowing the house is the Church itself. Trembling and amazed, Celano says, he rises and sets his whole heart on obeying. The prayer he made before that cross the Order keeps to this day.
stops.quote: Most High, glorious God, enlighten the darkness of my heart, and give me true faith, certain hope and perfect charity, sense and knowledge, Lord, that I may carry out Your holy and true command.
stops.quote_source: The Prayer before the Crucifix (Oratio ante crucifixum), earliest writings of Francis
suggested_refs: The San Damiano Crucifix, now in the Basilica of Santa Chiara, Assisi

stops.name: Foligno, the cloth and the horse sold
stops.campa: Obedient to the crucifix and still his father's son, Francesco loads a horse with scarlet cloth from the shop and rides to the market of Foligno, where he sells the cloth, and then, a merchant's flourish, sells the horse out from under himself. He walks the ten miles back and offers the whole purse to the poor priest of San Damiano for oil and stones. The priest, fearing Pietro di Bernardone, refuses the money; Francesco tosses it on a windowsill like dust, and asks instead to stay.
suggested_refs: The market square of Foligno; the money-window at San Damiano

stops.name: Assisi, the renunciation before the bishop
stops.campa: Pietro di Bernardone, whose chains in the cellar his wife undid, Pica loosing her son, hauls him before Bishop Guido in the court by Santa Maria Maggiore to disinherit him and recover the money. Francesco returns the coins, and then everything else: he strips naked before the whole city, lays his clothes at his father's feet, and the bishop wraps his mantle around him. From under the mantle the son declares the exchange of fathers. Afterward his mother consoles him: they share one name, Giovanna and Giovanni, one troubadour fire; he is always her son and a Bourlémont. He goes out from Assisi owning nothing, singing.
stops.quote: Until now I have called Pietro di Bernardone my father. From now on I can say freely: 'Our Father, who art in heaven,' since I have returned to him all his money and all my clothes.
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 20; Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 15
suggested_refs: Giotto, The Renunciation of Worldly Goods, Upper Basilica, Assisi
Piazza del Vescovado and Santa Maria Maggiore, Assisi

stops.name: The woods toward Gubbio, the herald of the great King
stops.campa: Wearing a hermit's cast-offs and singing the praises of God in French through the woods above Valfabbrica, Francesco is set upon by robbers. 'Who are you?' they demand. He gives them the answer of a man with nothing left to steal. They beat him, strip him of the poor cloak, and pitch him into a ditch full of snow. He climbs out, shakes off the snow, and goes on through the trees singing louder than before. The robbers have made the first audience of the new herald.
stops.quote: I am the herald of the great King! What is that to you?
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 16
suggested_refs: The Sentiero Francescano della Pace, Assisi to Gubbio, which follows this road

stops.name: Gubbio, the tunic of the Spadalonga
stops.campa: Half-frozen, having served as scullion at a monastery that gave him nothing but broth, Francesco reaches Gubbio and the house of his friend Federico Spadalonga, a merchant like his father. Federico clothes him: a plain tunic, a belt, shoes, the first garment freely given to the new poor man, and Gubbio never forgets that its cloth dressed the saint before his own city did. From here he goes among the lepers of the town, washing their sores with his own hands. The church of San Francesco della Pace rises later over the Spadalonga warehouse.
suggested_refs: Church of San Francesco, Gubbio, built over the Spadalonga house

stops.name: San Damiano, stones for a reward
stops.campa: Back beneath Assisi, Francesco turns mason. He begs stones in the streets like a jongleur crying wares, carries them on his shoulders that were never made for it, and rebuilds San Damiano with his own hands; then San Pietro della Spina in the fields; then the little ruin of Saint Mary of the Angels in the woods, the Porziuncola. Working on San Damiano he prophesies aloud, in French, that here will one day live ladies whose fame will glorify the whole Church. Clare is twelve years old, in the city above.
stops.quote: Whoever gives me one stone shall have one reward; whoever gives me two shall have two rewards; whoever gives me three, a triple reward!
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 21
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of San Damiano, Assisi, with the masonry of 1206
Testament of St. Clare, recording the prophecy of the Poor Ladies

stops.name: Porziuncola, the Gospel of the sending
stops.campa: On the feast of the apostle Matthias, at Mass in the little chapel he has rebuilt in the woods, Francesco hears the Gospel of the sending of the disciples: take no gold nor silver, no wallet for the road, no two tunics, no shoes, no staff. He asks the priest to expound it, and then cries out that this is what he has been looking for. On the spot he throws away shoes, staff and belt, ties his tunic with a cord, and becomes the thing the Gospel describes. The Order is born of one morning's reading.
stops.quote: This is what I want; this is what I seek; this is what I long to do with all my heart!
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 22
suggested_refs: The Porziuncola chapel, standing inside the Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli

stops.name: Assisi, San Nicolò, the triple opening of the Gospels
stops.campa: Bernard of Quintavalle, rich and respected, has watched Francesco pray the night through in his house and resolved to join him; Peter Catani, canon lawyer, comes with him. At dawn in the church of San Nicolò on the piazza the three hear Mass and then open the book of the Gospels three times to learn God's will: 'Sell all you have and give to the poor.' 'Take nothing for your journey.' 'Deny yourself, take up your cross.' Bernard sells everything that day and pours the money out in the piazza. The brotherhood exists.
stops.quote: Brothers, this is our life and our rule, and that of all who may wish to join our company. Go, therefore, and do as you have heard.
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 29
suggested_refs: The missal of San Nicolò, preserved at the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore, held to be the very book of the triple opening

stops.name: Poggio Bustone: 'Good day, good people!'
stops.campa: With his first brothers Francesco climbs into the Rieti valley and enters the mountain village of Poggio Bustone greeting everyone in the road, a greeting the town has repeated every morning since. In a cave above the village the certainty he has begged for is given him: his sins are forgiven, wholly, and he sees in a vision the multitude without number that will come after him into the little brotherhood: French, Spaniards, Germans, English, a great throng speaking every tongue. He comes down the mountain sure of both pardon and posterity.
stops.quote: Buon giorno, buona gente! — Good day, good people!
stops.quote_source: Local canon of Poggio Bustone, kept in the annual Festa del Buongiorno; cf. Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 26-27 for the vision
suggested_refs: The Sanctuary of Poggio Bustone and the upper grotto of the vision

stops.name: Rivotorto, the hovel of the brotherhood
stops.campa: The brothers, now a dozen, live crammed in an abandoned hovel by the twisting stream called Rivotorto, so narrow that Francesco chalks each brother's name on a beam to mark the place where he may sit and pray. They have no bread but turnips begged on the plain; they rejoice like men in a treasury. Here Francesco drafts the short first rule from the Gospel phrases. When a peasant drives his donkey into the shed to claim it, Francesco leads the brothers out without argument: poverty holds no leases, and they go to the Porziuncola.
suggested_refs: The Sanctuary of Rivotorto, enclosing a replica of the sacro tugurio, the holy hovel

stops.name: Rome, Innocent III and the dream of the falling Lateran
stops.campa: Twelve poor men stand before the most powerful pope in history. Innocent III has dreamed that the basilica of the Lateran, mother of all churches, was toppling, and that a small man in rags set his shoulder beneath it and held it up. Recognizing the beggar from his dream, he hears Francesco tell the parable of the poor woman wed by a great king, whose sons cannot be disowned. Cardinal John of St. Paul has argued their case; Innocent gives verbal approval to the way of life, and the tonsured brothers walk out with the Gospel for a rule.
stops.quote: There lived in the desert a woman who was poor but beautiful, whom a great king loved and married for her beauty; and her sons said: 'Do not be ashamed, for we are the sons of the King.'
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 16-17 (the parable Francis told Innocent III)
suggested_refs: Giotto, The Dream of Innocent III, Upper Basilica, Assisi

stops.name: Orte, the fortnight in the tombs
stops.campa: Walking home from Rome up the Tiber valley, the twelve stop near Orte and live a fortnight in an abandoned Etruscan tomb outside the walls, so happy in the sweetness of the place and of their new confirmation that they are tempted to stay forever and become hermits. Francesco weighs the hidden life against the command to preach, and chooses the roads: they were not called for themselves alone. The brotherhood leaves the tomb and walks north into the Spoleto valley to give itself away.
suggested_refs: The grotte of Orte above the Tiber bend

stops.name: Porziuncola, the Little Portion granted
stops.campa: Needing one church of their own, Francesco asks the Benedictine abbot of Monte Subasio for the smallest and poorest thing the abbey owns: Saint Mary of the Angels at the Little Portion, the Porziuncola in the oak woods. The monks give it, give it, but Francesco insists on paying rent, and every year sends the abbey a basket of small fish from the Rivotorto stream, so that the brothers may own nothing, not even their mother church. Here he fixes the heart of the Order; here he will ask to die.
suggested_refs: The Porziuncola within Santa Maria degli Angeli; the annual rent of lasche recorded in the tradition of Subasio

stops.name: Isola Maggiore, Lake Trasimeno, the fast of forty days
stops.campa: For Lent Francesco has a boatman set him alone on the wooded island of Trasimeno with two small loaves, telling no one but the friend who rows him. He keeps the whole forty days in a thicket, in prayer and against the frost, and when the boatman returns on Holy Thursday he finds one loaf untouched and half of the other eaten, the half-loaf eaten, the Fioretti says, out of reverence for Christ, that the fast of the sinner not presume to equal the fast of the sinless. The island keeps the memory in its Franciscan chapels.
suggested_refs: Isola Maggiore, Lake Trasimeno, and its chapel of the Sbarco di San Francesco

stops.name: Cannara, the town that would follow him whole
stops.campa: Francesco preaches in Cannara with such fire that the entire town, men, women, children, rises to abandon houses and fields and follow him on the road. He stops them: the world must not be emptied to fill the cloister. Stay, he tells them, marry, work, and I will ordain for you a way of penance inside your own walls. Out of this promise the tradition brings forth the Third Order, the brothers and sisters of penance living in the world; Cannara counts itself its cradle forever.
stops.quote: Do not be in haste, and do not leave; I will arrange what you should do for the salvation of your souls.
stops.quote_source: Fioretti 16
suggested_refs: Church of San Francesco, Cannara, and the town's title as cradle of the Third Order

stops.name: Piandarca, between Cannara and Bevagna, the sermon to the birds
stops.campa: On the plain called Piandarca, walking from Cannara toward Bevagna, Francesco lifts his eyes and sees the trees by the road filled with birds beyond counting. 'Wait for me here,' he tells his companions, 'while I go and preach to my sisters the birds.' He walks in among them; not one flies. He preaches; they stretch their necks, spread their wings, open their beaks, and touch his tunic with their heads. He signs them with the cross and they rise singing into the four quarters of the sky. From that day he calls all creatures brother and sister.
stops.quote: My brother birds, you ought greatly to praise your Creator and love Him always: He gave you feathers to wear, wings to fly, and whatever you need. God made you noble among His creatures and gave you a home in the purity of the air; you neither sow nor reap, and yet He protects and governs you without any care of your own.
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 58; Fioretti 16
suggested_refs: Giotto, The Sermon to the Birds, Upper Basilica, Assisi
The Edicola di Piandarca (1926) on the Cannara-Bevagna road

stops.name: Porziuncola, Clare's flight and tonsure
stops.campa: Palm Sunday night. Chiara di Favarone, eighteen, noble, leaves her father's palace by the door of the dead, the low door used only for corpses, and comes down through the olive groves to the torchlit Porziuncola, where the brothers wait with lamps. Before the altar of Saint Mary, Francesco cuts off her golden hair and clothes her in sackcloth and the veil: the Order of Poor Ladies begins. He shelters her with the nuns of San Paolo at Bastia, where her armed kinsmen fail to tear her from the altar cloths; soon she is set at San Damiano, as he prophesied while begging its stones.
suggested_refs: The reliquary of St. Clare's hair, Basilica of Santa Chiara, Assisi
The porta del morto of the Offreduccio house, Piazza San Rufino

stops.name: Alviano, the silencing of the swallows
stops.campa: At Alviano above the Tiber the whole town gathers to hear him, but the swallows nesting in the eaves are shrieking so that no one can hear a word. Francesco addresses them as he addresses everyone. The swallows fall silent at once and do not stir until the sermon is done. The people, Celano says, were amazed and gave glory to God; the fame of it runs through the valley faster than any bird.
stops.quote: My sisters the swallows, it is now time for me also to speak, since you have already said enough.
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 59
suggested_refs: The castle square of Alviano, where the sermon is localized

stops.name: The Dalmatian coast, shipwrecked toward Syria
stops.campa: Burning to preach to the Saracens or die a martyr, Francesco takes ship from Ancona for Syria, and contrary winds throw the vessel onto the coast of Slavonia, the Dalmatian shore. No ship will sail east so late in the year. Penniless, he and his companion stow away aboard a boat bound back for Ancona; a stranger, the canon knows who sends such strangers, has secretly stocked food for them, which multiplies through the storm-lengthened crossing and feeds the whole crew. The first assault on the East ends where it began, but the vow holds.
suggested_refs: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 55, the stowaway crossing and the multiplied provisions

stops.name: San Leo, the verse of the castle feast and the gift of La Verna
stops.campa: At the castle of San Leo in the Montefeltro, amid a great feast for a new knight, Francesco climbs onto a low wall and preaches on a verse of the troubadours he has made his own. Count Orlando Catani of Chiusi, pierced to the heart, draws him aside: he owns a mountain in Tuscany, La Verna, wild, solitary, fit for whoever would do penance far from the world, and he gives it to Francesco outright. Francesco sends two brothers to see it; they are met by fifty armed men against the wolves, and by falcons and a spring. The mountain waits eleven years for its wound.
stops.quote: So great is the good I have in sight, that every pain to me is a delight.
stops.quote_source: The First Consideration of the Holy Stigmata (appendix to the Fioretti)
suggested_refs: The fortress of San Leo, Montefeltro
The 1274 instrument of the donation of La Verna
sources: The Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, First Consideration

stops.name: Santiago de Compostela, the houses through all the world
stops.campa: Turned toward Morocco and the Miramamolin to preach and be martyred, Francesco crosses Spain and comes as a pilgrim to the tomb of Saint James at Compostela. Praying there through the night, it is revealed to him that he is to take many more places for his brothers: that the Order must spread its houses through all the world. Sickness meets him on the road and forbids Morocco; he obeys the illness as a message and turns back through Spain to Italy, leaving the tradition of a first friary in the city of the Apostle.
suggested_refs: Convento de San Francisco, Santiago de Compostela, founded by the pilgrim tradition of 1214

stops.name: Rome, the Fourth Lateran Council: Francis and Dominic
stops.campa: Innocent III opens the greatest council of the age in the Lateran, and Francesco is in Rome as it decrees that no new religious rules be invented; his own brotherhood, already blessed by word of mouth, slips through the closing door of history. Here the tradition sets his meeting with Dominic of Caléruega: the Spaniard has seen in vision two men presented to Christ by the Virgin, and recognizing the beggar from the vision, embraces him. 'You are my companion; let us stand together, and no adversary will prevail.' The two orders are brothers from that embrace.
suggested_refs: The meeting of Francis and Dominic, marble by Andrea della Robbia, Loggia di San Paolo, Florence
sources: Gerald of Frachet, Vitae Fratrum I.1

stops.name: Porziuncola, the Pentecost Chapter of the missions
stops.campa: At the Pentecost chapter of 1217 the brotherhood, grown past counting, divides the world like an inheritance. Provinces are drawn on the map of Christendom and beyond it: brothers to France, to Germany, to Hungary, to Spain, and across the sea to Syria under Brother Elias. Francesco himself sets out for France, land of his mother tongue of song, but at Florence Cardinal Ugolino, the Order's great protector and future Pope Gregory IX, turns him back: the head must not wander from the body. The Order becomes an army of the roads.
suggested_refs: The chapter grounds at Santa Maria degli Angeli

stops.name: Ancona, embarkation for the East
stops.campa: On the feast of Saint John the Baptist, Francesco sails at last from Ancona for the Crusade, with Peter Catani, Illuminato and a band of brothers. So many friars beg to go that he will not choose among them; he calls a child from the quay and lets the innocent finger pick the twelve who sail. The fleet runs by Cyprus to Acre, and from Acre down to the Nile, where the army of the Fifth Crusade lies rotting in its camp before Damietta. The little poor man goes to war carrying nothing.
suggested_refs: The old harbor of Ancona beneath Trajan's arch

stops.name: The camp before Damietta, the prophecy of defeat
stops.campa: In the crusader camp on the Nile, Francesco is shown the day's coming battle in prayer and is torn: if he speaks he will be called a fool, if he is silent his conscience will accuse him. He speaks. He walks the lines forbidding the attack in God's name; the barons laugh, the army advances on Damietta, and is cut to pieces, thousands of dead and captured by nightfall. Celano records the grief of the man of God over the slain, and the awe of an army that had laughed at him in the morning.
stops.quote: If the clash takes place today, the Lord has shown me that it will not go well for the Christians. But if I say so, they will call me a fool.
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 30
suggested_refs: The siege of Damietta in the Chronicle of Oliver of Paderborn

stops.name: Fariskur, the court of Sultan al-Kamil
stops.campa: During the truce Francesco and Brother Illuminato cross the lines toward the Saracen camp crying 'Soldan! Soldan!' They are seized, beaten, chained, and dragged before al-Malik al-Kamil, nephew of Saladin, who, expecting envoys or renegades, finds instead a small man in a patched habit offering to prove the Gospel by walking into fire with the sultan's own priests. The sultan will not light the fire, but he will not let him go: for days he keeps him, listening, and offers treasure that is refused. He sends him back with an escort, saying: 'Pray for me, that God may reveal to me the law most pleasing to Him.'
stops.quote: If you wish to be converted to Christ, you and your people, I shall most gladly stay with you for love of Him. But if you hesitate to abandon the law of Mohammed for the faith of Christ, then command that an enormous fire be lit, and I will enter the fire with your priests, that you may know which faith deserves to be held the holier and more certain.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure, Legenda Maior IX.8
suggested_refs: Giotto, The Trial by Fire before the Sultan, Bardi Chapel, Santa Croce, Florence
sources: Jacques de Vitry, Letter VI (1220), the eyewitness bishop's report

stops.name: Damietta taken, the grief in the victory
stops.campa: Damietta falls in the night of 5 November, falls without a battle, because plague and famine have already killed the city; the crusaders climb the walls into streets carpeted with the dead. Then comes the sack. Francesco, who had crossed the world to save souls on both sides of the wall, watches Christians fight Christians over plunder amid the corpses of Saracens, and the canon records his sorrow and his departure. He turns his back on the victory and goes up to Acre and the holy places, until word from Italy calls him home to a house in disorder.
suggested_refs: Oliver of Paderborn's Historia Damiatina on the fall of the city

stops.name: Porziuncola, the resignation at the Michaelmas chapter
stops.campa: Home from the East, where he heard that his vicars were altering the life, and where the sickness of his eyes began, Francesco gathers the chapter at Saint Mary of the Angels and does the thing no founder does: he lays down the government of his own Order before them all, kneeling, and names Peter Catani, and after Peter's death Brother Elias, to rule in his place. From now on he will command only by example. Henceforth he calls himself simply the little poor man, and asks of the Order one obedience: a brother assigned to be his own superior.
stops.quote: From now on I am dead to you. But here is Brother Peter di Catanio: let us all obey him, you and I.
stops.quote_source: Assisi Compilation 11; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 143
suggested_refs: The tomb of Peter Catani at the Porziuncola, dead within the year (10 March 1221)

segments.name: The Wolf, the Rule and the Crib

stops.name: Gubbio, the wolf at the Vittorina
stops.campa: A wolf of terrible size holds Gubbio in siege; it has eaten beasts and men, and the citizens go armed as to war. Francesco walks out of the gate against all pleading to where the wolf lives, by the place called the Vittorina. The wolf charges, jaws open; Francesco signs the cross and calls him Brother. The wolf closes his mouth, lies at his feet, and by the pledge of a lifted paw contracts the peace: he will harm no one, and Gubbio will feed him door to door. He keeps the pact two years, dies of old age, and is mourned; his grave lies under San Francesco della Pace.
stops.quote: Come here, Brother Wolf. I command you in the name of Christ that you do no harm to me nor to any man. Brother Wolf, since you are willing to make this peace and keep it, I promise you that the men of this town will feed you every day as long as you live, so that you shall never again suffer hunger.
stops.quote_source: Fioretti 21
suggested_refs: Sassetta, The Wolf of Gubbio, National Gallery, London
The wolf's grave-slab in San Francesco della Pace, Gubbio, with the skeleton found in 1872

stops.name: Porziuncola, the Chapter of Mats
stops.campa: Pentecost, and the plain around the Porziuncola becomes a city of wattle and rush: five thousand brothers encamped in huts of mats, whence the chapter takes its name. Francesco, his voice already failing, has Elias speak for him, sitting at his feet and tugging his tunic when he would add a word. The long Rule of 1221, woven through with the naked Gospel, is read to the multitude. In the crowd sits an unknown young Portuguese, lately of the Augustinian canons: Anthony, whom Padua will claim. The countryside feeds the whole swarm unbidden, and the brothers depart again into all the world.
suggested_refs: The Regula non bullata of 1221
The chapter fields of Santa Maria degli Angeli

stops.name: Bologna, the sermon of the Angels, Men and Demons
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption Francesco preaches in the piazza before the Palazzo Comunale of Bologna, city of lawyers, to almost the entire town. A student from Dalmatia, Thomas, later archdeacon of Split, stands in the crowd and writes down what he sees: a man in a ragged habit, unimpressive, unlettered, taking as his theme 'Angels, Men, Demons', and dividing it so finely that the learned marvel, while nobles who have been killing each other for generations make peace on the spot. It is the one sermon of Francesco's life caught by a bystander's pen.
suggested_refs: Thomas of Split, Historia Salonitana, the eyewitness paragraph on the Bologna sermon

stops.name: Fonte Colombo, the writing of the Rule
stops.campa: In the holy valley of Rieti, on the wooded slope of Fonte Colombo, the Sinai of the Order, Francesco fasts on bread and water with Brother Leo the scribe and Brother Bonizo the jurist, and dictates the final Rule in a cleft of the rock. The ministers climb the mountain to protest its severity; and from the air above the cave Christ's own voice answers them: 'Nothing in this Rule is Francis's; all of it is Mine, and I will that it be kept to the letter, to the letter, without gloss.' The ministers go back down the mountain in silence.
suggested_refs: The Sanctuary of Fonte Colombo, the Sacro Speco and the chapel of the Maddalena with Leo's tau

stops.name: Rome, Solet annuere: the Rule confirmed
stops.campa: On 29 November 1223 Pope Honorius III seals the bull Solet annuere and the Rule of the Lesser Brothers passes into the eternal law of the Church: twelve short chapters distilled from fourteen years of Gospel living, argued clause by clause at Cardinal Ugolino's side. What Innocent granted by word of mouth to twelve beggars, Honorius now grants under lead seal to an Order spread from England to Syria. The parchment itself returns to Assisi and lies in the Sacro Convento to this day.
stops.quote: The Rule and life of the Lesser Brothers is this: to observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience, without anything of one's own, and in chastity.
stops.quote_source: Regula bullata, chapter I (the Rule Francis dictated)
suggested_refs: The original bull Solet annuere with the Regula bullata, treasury of the Sacro Convento, Assisi
sources: Bull Solet annuere of Honorius III, 29 November 1223

stops.name: Greccio, the first nativity
stops.campa: Francesco sends for Giovanni Velita, lord of Greccio: prepare a manger in the cliff-cave, with hay, ox and ass. On the vigil night the mountainside blazes with torches as the people of the valley climb singing to the grotto; Mass is sung over the manger, and Francesco, in the deacon's dalmatic, chants the Gospel and preaches on the Babe of Bethlehem, pronouncing the word 'Bethlehem' like a bleating lamb. Among the pilgrims stands his cousin Pierre Bourlémont, holding the hand of twelve-year-old Joffrey. Giovanni sees a child asleep in the hay wake in Francesco's arms. The hay heals sick beasts; every crib in the world descends from this cave.
stops.quote: I want to enact the memory of that Child who was born in Bethlehem: to see, as far as is possible with my own bodily eyes, the hardship of his infant needs, how he lay in a manger, and how, with an ox and an ass standing by, he rested on hay.
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 84
suggested_refs: Giotto, The Crib at Greccio, Upper Basilica, Assisi
The grotto chapel of the Presepe, Sanctuary of Greccio

stops.name: La Verna, the seraph and the stigmata
stops.campa: For the fast of Saint Michael, Francesco keeps to Orlando's mountain with Leo and three brothers, lodged alone past a chasm. At the Exaltation of the Cross, praying at dawn, he sees a seraph with six wings of fire descend, and between the wings the figure of the Crucified. When the vision withdraws, the wounds remain: nails of his own flesh through hands and feet, and in his side an open wound that bleeds. The count is his mother's: the Khamsa Pierre sang into Pica, the five sufferings become five wounds. He hides them under bandages; to Leo, who dresses them, he gives the chartula written in his own hand.
stops.quote: You are holy, Lord, the only God, and Your deeds are wonderful. You are strong. You are great. You are the Most High. You are love. You are wisdom. You are humility. You are endurance. You are beauty. You are our eternal life, great and wonderful Lord, God almighty, merciful Savior. — May the Lord bless you and keep you; may He show His face to you and be merciful to you. May the Lord bless you, Brother Leo.
stops.quote_source: The Chartula of Assisi: the Praises of God and the Blessing for Brother Leo, autograph of Francis, written on La Verna, September 1224
suggested_refs: The autograph chartula with the Blessing for Brother Leo, reliquary chapel, Sacro Convento, Assisi
The Chapel of the Stigmata, Sanctuary of La Verna
sources: The Considerations on the Holy Stigmata, Third Consideration
essays/207_hebraic_knots.md (the five sufferings of the Khamsa and the five wounds of La Verna)

stops.name: Borgo San Sepolcro, carried through the town unseeing
stops.campa: Coming down from La Verna on a borrowed donkey, too wounded now to walk far, Francesco passes through Borgo San Sepolcro, where the whole town pours out and the crowd presses to touch him, cutting pieces from his tunic. He notices none of it: rapt out of his senses, he rides through the shouting streets as through an empty field, and only long after, when the brothers speak of the town, does he ask his companions the question the canon treasures as proof of where he truly traveled that day.
stops.quote: When shall we come to Borgo?
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 98
suggested_refs: The hermitage of Montecasale above Sansepolcro, his lodging on this road

stops.name: San Damiano, the Canticle of the Creatures
stops.campa: Nearly blind, his eyes unable to bear daylight or firelight, tormented by field-mice in the night, Francesco lies fifty days in a dark cell of mats beside San Damiano, where Clare and her ladies tend him. There, at the bottom of pain, he is assured in prayer of the kingdom, and rises to compose not a lament but the great doxology of the world: the Canticle of Brother Sun, the first great poem of the Italian tongue, and sets the brothers to sing it. He, who cannot bear the sun on his eyes, praises the sun first of all creatures.
stops.quote: Most High, all-powerful, good Lord, Yours are the praises, the glory, the honor and all blessing. Praised be You, my Lord, with all Your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who is the day, and through whom You give us light; and he is beautiful and radiant with great splendor. Praised be You, my Lord, through Sister Moon and the stars. Praised be You, my Lord, through Brother Wind, and through the air, cloudy and serene, and every weather. Praised be You, my Lord, through Sister Water, who is very useful and humble and precious and chaste. Praised be You, my Lord, through Brother Fire, by whom You light the night. Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Mother Earth, who sustains and governs us, and produces varied fruits with colored flowers and herbs.
stops.quote_source: The Canticle of the Creatures (Canticle of Brother Sun), composed at San Damiano, 1225
suggested_refs: The Canticle in MS 338 of the Biblioteca del Sacro Convento, Assisi, the oldest copy
The garden of the Canticle at San Damiano

stops.name: La Foresta, the miracle of the vintage
stops.campa: Summoned to Rieti for the treatment of his eyes, Francesco waits at the priest's small church of San Fabiano above the town, and the crowds that come to see the stigmatized saint trample the little vineyard flat and strip the grapes: the priest's whole living. Francesco asks him what the vineyard yields in its best year: thirteen measures. He promises twenty for the ruined vintage. The half-wrecked vines that autumn press out twenty measures of wine and more, and the place takes the name La Foresta and keeps the story with the wine-vat still shown there.
suggested_refs: The Sanctuary of La Foresta, Rieti, with the traditional wine-press of the miracle

stops.name: Fonte Colombo, Brother Fire and the cautery
stops.campa: The physicians of the papal court at Rieti decree the last remedy for his eyes: the cautery, a rod of iron drawn glowing from temple to eyebrow. At Fonte Colombo the brothers flee the room rather than watch. Francesco addresses the fire in the brazier as an old friend and kinsman, signs it with the cross, and when the searing iron has hissed across his living flesh he calls the brothers back, laughing at them: 'If it is not well burned, let him burn it again.' He has felt, he says, neither the fire's heat nor any pain in his flesh. Brother Fire kept courtesy.
stops.quote: My Brother Fire, noble and useful among all the creatures the Most High has created, be courteous to me in this hour, for I have always loved you and always will for the love of Him who created you. And I pray our Creator who made you, to temper your heat now, so that I may bear it.
stops.quote_source: Assisi Compilation 86; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 166
suggested_refs: The Sanctuary of Fonte Colombo, chapel of the cauterization

stops.name: Siena: blood in the night, the little testament
stops.campa: Taken to Siena for yet more doctors, Francesco vomits blood through a whole night, and the brothers, certain the end has come, beg a word to remember him by. He cannot write; he was never able to say things at length any more; so he dictates to Brother Benedict of Piratro the three sentences that the Order calls the Siena Testament: blessing, love among brothers, fidelity to Lady Poverty and to the Church. Then, refusing to die anywhere but at Saint Mary of the Angels, he sets his face toward Assisi by way of Cortona.
stops.quote: Write that I bless all my brothers, those who are in the Order and those who will come until the end of the world. Let them always love one another; let them always love and observe our Lady holy Poverty; and let them always be faithful and subject to the prelates and all clerics of holy Mother Church.
stops.quote_source: The Siena Testament, dictated to Brother Benedict of Piratro, April 1226
suggested_refs: The Siena Testament in the Assisi Compilation 59

stops.name: Le Celle di Cortona, the hermitage above the gorge
stops.campa: On the road home the dying man rests at the cells above Cortona, the hermitage he founded in the gorge of the torrent fifteen years before, where Brother Elias now keeps his cave. The dropsy has begun: his legs and belly swell as his sight fails. In the stone cell by the water, still shown, unchanged, narrow as a ship's berth, the tradition of Cortona holds that he set in order the thoughts that will become the great Testament. When he is carried on toward Assisi, the escort swings wide through Gubbio, for Perugia would steal a dying saint for the sake of his bones.
suggested_refs: The cell of St. Francis at the Eremo Le Celle, Cortona

stops.name: Bagnara above Nocera, the knights and the begged supper
stops.campa: Against the summer heat of the plain he is carried up to Bagnara in the hills by Nocera, where the brothers have a new house among the springs. His body swells; the end is plainly near. Assisi, terrified that some other city will possess his relics, sends knights of the commune to bring him home under arms. On the road, at the poor village of Satriano, the knights can buy nothing for supper; Francesco smiles and sends them begging for the love of God, and doors that money could not open, open. The soldiers of Assisi come back fed and instructed.
stops.quote: Go and beg alms from door to door for the love of the Lord God — you found nothing for money, but for the love of God you will find everything.
stops.quote_source: Assisi Compilation 96; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 77
suggested_refs: The site of Satriano on the Nocera-Assisi road, with the annual Cavalcata di Satriano retracing the knights' escort

stops.name: Assisi, the bishop's palace and the strophe of pardon
stops.campa: Lodged under guard in the palace of the bishop, dying in the city of his birth, Francesco hears that Bishop Guido and the podestà Oportulo have excommunicated and banned each other, and that Assisi is tearing itself in two. He cannot walk to make peace, so he makes a verse: a new strophe for the Canticle, on pardon, and sends the brothers to sing it before bishop and podestà together in the cloister court. The podestà weeps and kneels; the bishop begs forgiveness and embraces him. The city is reconciled by a song: the poem doing, in his last month, the work of his whole life.
stops.quote: Praised be You, my Lord, through those who give pardon for Your love, and bear infirmity and tribulation. Blessed are those who endure in peace, for by You, Most High, they shall be crowned.
stops.quote_source: The Canticle of the Creatures, the strophe of pardon, added at Assisi, 1226 (Assisi Compilation 84)
suggested_refs: The cloister of the Vescovado, Assisi, where the strophe was sung

stops.name: The road to the Porziuncola, the blessing of Assisi
stops.campa: Knowing Sister Death is at the door, he asks to be carried down to Saint Mary of the Angels, to die where the Order was born. At the crossroads by the leper-house, halfway down the plain, he asks the bearers to halt and turn the litter so that his face is toward Assisi, the city he can no longer see. He raises himself and blesses it, walls, towers and people, with the blessing the canon has kept word for word; then he is carried on down into the oak woods, and Assisi stands blessed above the plain forever.
stops.quote: Lord, as of old this city was the abode of wicked and unjust men, so now may it be the abode and dwelling of those who know You, glorify Your name, and give forth the fragrance of pure life and good renown to all Christian people. May it please You that it remain always the home of those who know and glorify Your blessed and glorious name for ever and ever. Amen.
stops.quote_source: Mirror of Perfection 124; Assisi Compilation
suggested_refs: Casa Gualdi, the traditional site of the blessing on the Assisi-Porziuncola road

stops.name: Porziuncola, Sister Death
stops.campa: In the infirmary hut beside the Porziuncola he adds the last strophe to the Canticle, the welcome to Sister Bodily Death, and has the brothers sing it over him. He dictates his Testament; the Lady Jacopa arrives from Rome unsummoned, forewarned from heaven, bringing the almond cakes he craved. He has bread broken and given to all in memory of the Supper, has the Passion read from John, and is laid naked on the naked earth. At dusk on Saturday, 3 October 1226, singing Psalm 141, he dies; and a great multitude of larks, birds of the light, wheel low over the hut, singing in the dark.
stops.quote: Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living man can escape. Woe to those who die in mortal sin; blessed are those whom she finds in Your most holy will, for the second death shall do them no harm. — I have done what was mine to do; may Christ teach you what is yours!
stops.quote_source: The Canticle of the Creatures, final strophe; Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda 214
suggested_refs: The Cappella del Transito, Santa Maria degli Angeli, the hut where he died
The Testament of St. Francis

stops.name: Assisi, San Giorgio, the burial, and the window of San Damiano
stops.campa: At dawn the whole city comes down with olive branches and torches to carry him home in triumph: the first procession of a feast the world will keep on this day forever. By his own last wish the cortege turns aside to San Damiano, and the grated window is opened so that Clare and her ladies may see him once more and kiss the wounded hands: the stigmata, hidden in life, shown openly in death. Then the city buries him at San Giorgio, where he learned his letters and first preached, until Elias's great basilica is ready, and Gregory IX, his friend Ugolino, writes him among the saints.
suggested_refs: The window of the transit at San Damiano
The tomb of St. Francis, rediscovered 1818, in the crypt of the Basilica di San Francesco
